newsitem.title: USA: Texaco releases plan to promote fairness.
newsitem.headline: Texaco releases plan to promote fairness.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

Texaco Inc., engulfed in scandal over alleged racial discrimation, released a plan on Wednesday to boost employment of minorities and purchasing from minority companies but said it was not setting quotas.
The plan follows the company's agreement last month to settle a racial discrimation suit by paying $176.1 million and establishing an "equality and tolerance" task force.
The proposed settlement still needs a judge's approval and a hearing on the matter has been set for Jan. 3 in a federal court in White Plains, N.Y., where Texaco is based.
The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which has asked to intervene in the case, had no comment on the diversity plan from the nation's third largest oil company.
Cyrus Mehri, one of the lawyers representing plaintiffs in the discrimination case, praised Texaco for the plan.

"The company has some laudable plans here, many of which are required by our settlement," said Mehri, of the Washington, D.C., firm of Cohen, Milstein, Hausfeld & Toll. "We commend the company for moving forward on an expedited basis even before the settlement becomes final."
The accord calls for Texaco to fulfil the settlement requirements within six months of approval.
The Rev. Jesse Jackson also found the plan acceptable and called for an end to the consumer boycott of Texaco he helped initiate last month.

"We now have a sufficiently comprehensive and workable plan to call an end to the consumer boycott," Jackson said at a news conference. "Texaco is on a journey from tragedy to triumph. The journey is incomplete but they have changed their course."
The National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People also called off its campaign for stockholders to divest Texaco stock.

Texaco's plan lists a broad range of initiatives providing for increased employment of women and minorities, programmes to aid them in obtaining promotions, methods for reporting employment complaints and provisions to link managers' salaries with their performance in creating an open workplace.

"Based on our review, we have set ... initiatives that are well-balanced and beneficial to all our employees and bring us a critical competitive advantage," Chief Executive Officer Peter Bijur said in a statement.

"The goals of our programme were set by determining what the demographics of Texaco's work force are likely to be in the year 2000. And, to be clear, these are goals -- they are not quotas," he added.
Texaco said that through previous efforts it has increased minority employment from 16 percent in 1991 to 23 percent and expects to reach 29 percent by the end of 2000.
Also by that time, Texaco expects that blacks will make up 13 percent of its work force, up from 9 percent, and 35 percent, up from 32 percent.
"These increases will take place in the context of modest overall employment growth during this period," Texaco said.
The plan calls for expanded recruiting efforts, including a new scholarship programme to develop minority students for management careers at Texaco.
Texaco also plans to boost its purchasing from minority- and women-owned businesses from $135 million in 1996 to more than $1 billion over the next five years.

It plans to boost financial activities with minority- and women-owned banks and money managers from $32 million to $200 million and its coverage from minority- and women-owned insurance companies from $25 million to $200 million.
The company plans to address career development of women and minorities and will establish a mentoring programme linking managers and senior professionals with aspiring employees.

The company said it will also develop programmes to create a more open and inclusive environment at Texaco, such as including women and minorities on human resource committees and setting alternative ways to resolve disputes.

Problems at Texaco surfaced last month after plantiffs' lawyers in the discrimination suit received secret tapes of senior executives discussing the destruction of damaging documents. The executives allegedly also made racist remarks.

Richard Lundwall, former senior coordinator of personnel services of Texaco's finance department, had the tapes of himself and other officers. He gave the plaintiffs' lawyers the tapes after he was forced out of the company.

Last month Lundwall, 55, of Danbury, Conn., was charged with obstruction of justice in a one-count criminal complaint filed by prosecutors. According to court papers released on Tuesday, his lawyer is in negotiations with prosecutors.
